planting.note: Direct sow onto loose, exposed sand in fall and leave the seed uncovered, since burial depth and ongoing sand disturbance are what trigger this species' germination and spread.

directions: Blowout grass is the signature pioneer of active sand blowouts in the Nebraska Sandhills, sending out long, cord-like rhizomes several feet through loose, shifting sand to anchor the dune face before almost any other plant can take hold. Its narrow, rolled, pale blue-green leaves and open, feathery panicles emerge from bare sand that would bury most other grasses, and the plant actually grows faster when partially buried by drifting sand. Direct sow seed onto loose, exposed sand in fall and leave it uncovered, since this species germinates and spreads in response to ongoing sand movement rather than stable ground. It needs no irrigation or fertility once established and is best used for erosion control on bare dune faces or sand blowouts rather than as a conventional garden grass.

subcategory: Nebraska Sandhills blowout endemic, rare conservation-priority

planting.note: Sow fresh seed in fall onto bare, loose sand so it overwinters outdoors and receives the cold stratification it needs, since this rare species only establishes on actively shifting, largely unvegetated dune sand.

directions: Blowout penstemon is a federally threatened species found at only a handful of active sand blowouts in the Nebraska Sandhills and a small disjunct population in south-central Wyoming, where its thick, waxy, blue-gray leaves and spreading underground stems let it colonize the same loose, shifting sand that defeats most other wildflowers. Large, pale lavender-blue tubular flowers open in late spring on stems that rarely rise far above the surrounding sand, and the species depends on continued sand movement and sparse competing vegetation to persist. Because wild populations are so limited, seed and plants are realistically obtainable only in small quantities through university and conservation-nursery restoration programs rather than general retail sources, and material should be sourced only through those programs. In a conservation or restoration planting, give it full sun, bare loose sand, and no irrigation or fertilizer, since stable, vegetated, or fertile ground causes it to decline and disappear.

subcategory: Nebraska Sandhills sand prairie pioneer annual

planting.note: Direct sow around the last frost date onto loose, bare, lean sandy soil in full sun, since this pioneer annual germinates best on fresh, disturbed sand rather than among established vegetation.

directions: James' clammyweed (also listed in older references as Cristatella jamesii) is a sticky-glandular, strong-scented native annual that colonizes bare, shifting sand on blown-out dune faces and sandy riverbanks across the Nebraska Sandhills and central Great Plains, often appearing in the same disturbed openings as blowout grass and sand dropseed. Its slender, sticky stems carry narrow trifoliate leaves and loose clusters of small, four-petaled white to pale pink flowers with long, showy stamens that open through summer and into early fall. As a true pioneer annual it depends on open, unvegetated sand and will not persist once grasses and other perennials close in the ground, so it works best scattered on fresh, disturbed sand rather than in an established bed. Direct sow in spring onto loose, lean sandy soil and skip supplemental watering and fertilizer, which favor weedy competitors over this short-lived specialist.

planting.note: Scarify the hard seed coat lightly and direct sow in fall into lean, well-drained sandy soil, since this deep-rooted legume forms a taproot almost immediately and resents later transplanting.

directions: Lemon scurfpea is a wiry, deep-rooted native legume of loose sand prairie and dune grassland across the Nebraska Sandhills and central Great Plains, where its silvery, gland-dotted foliage and extensive root system let it thrive in soil too loose and infertile for most other forbs. Crushed leaves and stems release a distinctive lemony, resinous scent, and small clusters of pale blue-violet, pea-like flowers appear along the upper stems from late spring into summer. Like other wild scurfpeas, it fixes its own nitrogen and should never be planted in rich or amended soil, which lets weedy competitors overtake it. Scarify seed lightly and direct sow into lean, well-drained sandy soil in fall, since the long taproot forms quickly and the plant does not transplant well once established.

planting.note: Direct sow into lean, loose, sandy soil in spring once soil has warmed, giving plants ample room since established stands spread steadily outward from rhizomes over several seasons.

directions: Sand bluestem is the dune-adapted counterpart of big bluestem, forming large, rhizomatous clumps of blue-green summer foliage topped by the same distinctive forked, turkey-foot seed heads, but on a plant built to thrive in loose, droughty Sandhills sand rather than heavier prairie loam. Its extensive rhizome system and deep roots let it stabilize open dune slopes and blowout margins while still producing the tall, airy fall structure prized in native grass plantings, with foliage turning coppery orange-red after frost. Direct sow into lean, sandy, well-drained soil in spring, giving plants ample room since established stands spread steadily outward from their rhizomes over several seasons. It needs no irrigation or fertilizer once established and is a staple seed-mix component for Sandhills range restoration as well as large-scale native grass gardens.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall into loose, well-drained sandy soil and leave undisturbed, since this long-lived species develops a deep, woody taproot almost immediately and seedlings rarely survive being dug or transplanted.

directions: Hairy puccoon is a larger, showier relative of the narrowleaf puccoon found on loess bluffs, instead favoring the deep, loose sand of dune prairie and blowout margins across the Great Plains, where its coarse, bristly-hairy stems and leaves help it withstand the sun and wind exposure of open dunes. It opens clusters of bright orange-yellow, fragrant trumpet flowers from late spring into early summer that are considerably larger and showier than those of its narrowleaf cousin. Like other puccoons, it develops a deep, woody, dye-bearing taproot almost immediately after germination and should always be seeded directly where it is to grow rather than transplanted. Direct sow in fall into loose, well-drained sandy soil in full sun and avoid rich or irrigated ground, which shortens its naturally long life in the wild.

subcategory: Nebraska Sandhills sand prairie annual, wildlife food plant

planting.note: Direct sow into lean, sandy, disturbed or recently tilled soil after the last frost, since seed germinates readily on bare ground but is quickly shaded out once grasses close in.

directions: Texas croton, widely known among upland bird hunters as doveweed, is a bushy, grayish-green native annual that colonizes disturbed, sandy ground across the Nebraska Sandhills and southern Great Plains, releasing a sharp, skunky odor when the foliage is crushed or bruised. Its small, inconspicuous flowers give way through late summer to abundant tiny seeds that are a key late-season food source for mourning doves and other seed-eating birds, which is why the species is deliberately seeded into wildlife food plots and disked field margins. Direct sow into lean, sandy soil in disturbed or tilled ground after the last frost, since the seed germinates readily on bare soil but faces heavy competition once grasses close in. It needs no irrigation or fertilizer and is best used in a dedicated wildlife planting or disturbed-sand restoration area rather than a conventional flower bed.

planting.note: Direct sow or set out small transplants in spring into lean, loose, sandy soil in full sun, avoiding heavy clay or regularly irrigated ground where the roots are prone to rot.

directions: Sand sagebrush is a low, finely textured, aromatic shrub with thread-like silvery-gray foliage that forms loose colonies across the open sand prairie and dune grassland of the Nebraska Sandhills and southern Great Plains, often growing alongside yucca and sand bluestem on wind-exposed ridges. Crushed foliage releases a sharp, resinous sage scent, and small, inconspicuous flower heads appear on upright stems in late summer and fall, adding winter structure and silvery contrast rather than showy bloom. It spreads slowly by seed and short rhizomes rather than aggressively, and its deep, wide-ranging root system makes it extremely drought tolerant once established. Direct sow or transplant small plants into lean, loose, sandy soil in full sun, and avoid heavy clay or regularly irrigated sites where the roots are prone to rot.
